themes.definition: Guidance, tools, certification and staff skills for securing AI systems and the data around them.
themes.what_is_set_out: NCSC is the main provider pointed to: principles for securing machine-learning solutions (UK174, UK139), guidelines for secure AI system development (via security.gov.uk in AI_Insights; also UK099), the Cyber Assessment Framework (UK099), resources, courses and Cyber Essentials certification (UK206), and guidance on intelligent security tools (UK010); UK099 also points to the Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI, and UK174 tells teams they 'should use' the Technology Code of Practice and NCSC cloud security principles. UK174 also lists non-state sources (Microsoft's list of ML failure modes, MITRE ATLAS, OWASP). On skills, UK268 lists training staff 'to recognise security threats' as a possible control, and UK010 says it will be 'necessary' to keep cyber-security management and technical teams' skills up to date with developments in AI. AI_Insights mentions vendors' vulnerability updates. Two passages concern AI used against the organisation, or by it for defence, rather than the body's own AI tool: UK174 on educating users 'to detect AI-produced fake messages' (flagged by the coders as an edge case) and UK010 on AI-based defensive security tools.
themes.holders: Providers: NCSC, security.gov.uk, and non-state sources (Microsoft, MITRE, OWASP, vendors). Holders of skills requirements: 'you' (UK174), the organisation (UK268), stakeholders (UK010).
themes.binding: Pointers, plus 'should use' (UK174), 'You’ll also need to' (UK174), 'necessary' (UK010), 'possible control' (UK268). All non-statutory; no consequence is stated.
themes.checks: n/a: no security test of an AI tool or its outputs is specified in these passages (checks on AI-written code are under 'Testing, evaluation and explainability tools').

themes.theme: Technical environments, platforms, sandboxes and compute
themes.definition: Hosting infrastructure, development and test environments, enterprise platforms, sandboxes and computing power needed to build, test or run AI tools.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 asks organisations to 'consider providing' data and digital professionals with sandboxes to experiment securely, and warns that self-hosting a model means 'you must also maintain the infrastructure', with extra costs and ML-operations skills. AI_Insights says an organisation applying AI to its records 'needs access to' a development or sandbox environment and enough data; it notes that some AI tool providers and vendor-neutral sandboxes supply environments, that cloud-suite AI tools or software-as-a-service licences may provide the needed functions, and lists required functions including the ability to 'maintain an audit trail of actions on content'; it also notes that some debiasing methods need 'substantial computational resources'. The NAO commits to stand up secure enterprise AI platforms and to 'Roll out Copilot and core AI tooling within guardrails'. Regulator sandboxes appear as a general mention (UK206) and as Ofgem's proposed AI technical sandbox for testing and evaluating AI 'before any live deployment' (UK010; decision pending at publication). UK082 recommends sovereign compute for critical services, a data-rich experimentation environment and a scalable AI tech stack for 'tens or hundreds of millions of citizen interactions'.
themes.holders: The organisation / 'you' (UK174, AI_Insights); the NAO for its own staff; regulators and Ofgem as sandbox providers, energy-sector participants as users (UK010, UK206); government or the public sector (UK082 recommendations); commercial providers named as sources (Microsoft, Google, cloud and LLM providers).
themes.binding: Mixed: UK174 'consider' (sandboxes) and a conditional 'must' (if self-hosting) in non-statutory guidance; AI_Insights 'needs access to'; NAO commitments; Ofgem's sandbox a proposal; UK082 recommendations whose acceptance is not recorded. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Ofgem sandbox (UK010, proposed): trigger: before live deployment; compared against: not stated; metric: not stated; who: energy-sector participants 'with proportionate regulatory oversight'; result: not stated. AI_Insights' audit-trail function supports recording of actions on content but no check is described. Otherwise n/a.

themes.theme: Money: funding, budgets and whole-life costs
themes.definition: Statements about who pays for delivering and assuring AI, and the costs public bodies are told to anticipate.
themes.what_is_set_out: Money is mostly something the public body must find, and no passage gives an amount. UK206 lists as a core governance process ensuring that 'AI assurance capability and infrastructure is adequately funded'; UK099 asks teams to consider what resources to make available across the life cycle 'to fix newly identified fairness problems and to remediate harms'; AI_Insights asks that 'budgets and resources are available for ongoing training'; UK133 asks for evaluation resources at the planning stage; UK136 says the cost of continued support 'should be factored in when purchasing'; UK174 notes that self-hosting 'brings additional costs'. Funding offered by central government is limited to the Government Office for Technology Transfer, which 'can provide support and funding to help develop government-wide solutions' (UK174), and grant challenges for bias and fairness tools run by DSIT or CDEI with Innovate UK (UK139, UK206). UK082 recommends significant investment in assurance tools (including AISI's fast grants), continued support for AISI, central funding for scaling successful pilots, and pay for AI roles benchmarked to at least 75% of the private-sector rate; these are recommendations whose acceptance is not recorded.
themes.holders: Organisations, teams and buyers (as payers); the Government Office for Technology Transfer, DSIT/CDEI with Innovate UK (as funders); government and AISI (UK082 recommendations).
themes.binding: 'Should', 'consider', 'baseline' governance process, 'it is important'; funding offers ('can provide'); UK082 recommendations. No consequence is stated.

themes.theme: Central capability and support offers to public bodies
themes.definition: Support that central government bodies (DSIT, AISI, CDEI, the Government Office for Technology Transfer) offer, or are recommended to offer, to public bodies or regulators for building, testing and assuring AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: Most of this is recommendation. UK082 proposes that DSIT 'should support public sector partners where needed', a rapid prototyping capability with 'technical and delivery resource to build and test proof of concepts', support to hire external AI talent, a data-rich experimentation environment, a scaling service with central funding, a scalable AI tech stack, and continued growth of AISI's model-evaluation research; acceptance is not recorded in the document. Existing or committed offers are fewer: support and funding from the Government Office for Technology Transfer (UK174); DSIT's central function supplying 'expert risk analysis' to help regulators assess AI risks (UK139); and the CDEI's commitment to 'embed assurance thinking' in partnership projects with defence-focused organisations, police forces and local authorities (UK207), which the coders note is the one passage in that roadmap aimed at public-sector AI. UK206's statement that AISI 'will offer novel tools and systems' concerns frontier AI risks rather than public bodies' own tools.
themes.holders: DSIT, AISI, government (UK082); Government Office for Technology Transfer (UK174); DSIT's central function, for regulators (UK139); CDEI (UK207); AISI (UK206). themes.theme: Resources secured from suppliers through procurement and contracts
themes.definition: Information, training, staff and compliance work that public bodies are told to obtain from suppliers, or that suppliers and framework operators provide.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several documents place the source of delivery resources with the supplier. UK010 says users 'should be able to access information regarding what and where the AI is used, its characteristics, any failure modes and necessary risk control measures', including, per the coder note, how to identify incorrect or misleading results. EHRC (UK216) recommends that contracts require the supplier to provide monitoring information. UK206 notes that an organisation evaluating a system 'may need to ensure' access to documentation about the system design and management processes. UK136 tells buyers to make knowledge transfer, training and explanations for non-specialists part of the requirement, and to require the supplier to assemble a team with the right skills and diversity 'to mitigate bias in the AI system'. DWP (UK190) requires contract managers to ensure suppliers know their responsibilities when using AI tools. The Crown Commercial Service carries out 'Thorough ongoing supplier compliance checks', so buyers 'have less to do at call-off' (UK174). AI_Insights mentions learning credits in strategic-partner contracts, and UK085 mentions vendor model cards and white papers. No passage here says suppliers must disclose test results, model versions or performance on the buyer's own data.
themes.holders: The supply chain and suppliers (UK010, UK216, UK136); buyers: central government departments (UK136), public bodies (UK216), the organisation evaluating (UK206); DWP contract managers (UK190); Crown Commercial Service (UK174); strategic partners (AI_Insights); vendors (UK085).
themes.binding: UK190 'must' in a departmental policy; UK136 imperatives in guidance; UK010 'should'; UK216 a recommended contractual requirement; UK206 'may need to'; others provided or mentioned. No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Crown Commercial Service supplier compliance checks (UK174): trigger: ongoing, for framework suppliers; compared against: compliance requirements, not specified; metric: not stated; who: CCS; result: buyers have less to do at call-off. themes.theme: Non-state assurance ecosystem: market, research and professional bodies
themes.definition: Assurance providers, research bodies, civil-society groups and professional bodies outside government that are described as supplying assurance skills, tools, training or certification.
themes.what_is_set_out: The two DSIT/CDEI assurance documents rest the supply of assurance largely on a market. UK207 states that 'A trustworthy market of assurance providers is needed to provide specialist skills for AI assurance and independent oversight' and that 'a toolbox of different products, services and standards is required', framed in the ministerial foreword as 'a market-based complement to more formal regulation'. UK206 reports 'a growing market of AI assurance providers', research bodies (the Alan Turing Institute, the University of York) developing tools, the Ada Lovelace Institute's template algorithmic impact assessment for healthcare, and professional bodies: the International Association of Algorithmic Auditors 'hoping to' create a code of conduct, curricula and eventually certification, and the IAPP offering training and certification; per the coder notes, UK206 also records that there are currently no professional bodies with Chartered Status focused on AI assurance. These passages describe what exists or is hoped for; they do not say public bodies must use outside assurance, nor how its quality is to be judged.
themes.holders: Assurance providers, research bodies (Alan Turing Institute, University of York), civil society (Ada Lovelace Institute), professional bodies (IAAA, IAPP), the AI Standards Hub; recipients: organisations and 'those building, deploying and using AI'.
themes.binding: Descriptive, or aspirational ('is needed', 'is required', 'We will also need'). No consequence.
themes.checks: UK207 assigns 'independent oversight' to assurance providers: trigger, comparator, metric and what happens with the result are not stated. Otherwise n/a.

absences: No Resources starting code is wholly missing: roles and staff, skills and training, money, time, tools, templates, data, access, information and outside support (including non-state providers) all have passages. Several are thin. Time appears only as UK174's five-day learning entitlement and general calls for 'time and resources'. Money never comes with an amount and, apart from the Government Office for Technology Transfer and grant challenges, appears as costs the public body must bear or as UK082 recommendations. Measured against the Delivery activities this cell is meant to resource, logging and recording are almost unresourced (an audit-trail function and tooling to record review decisions in AI_Insights; logging protocols in the Turing framework that UK136 points to). A reader would expect, but does not find: reference or 'ground truth' data against which a public body could check a tool's outputs on its own task; any resource for testing whether outputs are consistent or repeatable, for tracking model versions, prompts or configuration, or for re-testing after a model update; confidence thresholds, sampling rates or staffing levels for human review; a central testing or evaluation service available to public bodies now (AISI's model evaluations concern frontier models, and UK082's government-backed assurance tools are a recommendation); and any statutory duty to resource delivery. Most of what is 'provided' is documents, catalogues and pointers to commercial or open-source tools, not people, money or infrastructure.
cross_cutting: This cell is dominated by people and skills (who should be on the team, what staff should be trained in, how to keep capability in-house) and by long lists of guidance, toolkits, standards and commercial tools that the documents point to. Almost everything is required of the public body itself ('you', 'the organisation', 'teams', 'stakeholders') rather than provided to it; where something is provided, it is mostly a document or catalogue (the Playbook, AI Insights, the Portfolio of AI assurance techniques, ICO and EHRC toolkits, the ATRS template), while staff, money and infrastructure appear chiefly as UK082 recommendations or as the NAO's commitments for its own staff. The cell is almost entirely non-statutory: the verbs are 'should', 'consider' and 'can', with 'must' in UK174 and UK136 (guidance) and in DWP's departmental policy (UK190); no document states a consequence for failing to resource delivery, though UK268 names the resulting risks. UK207 and UK206 rest much of the supply of assurance on an outside market, UK174 accepts contractors because of the talent shortage, and UK266 warns against treating AI as an outsourced issue, so the documents differ on whether checking capability should sit inside the public body [inference]. On checking AI outputs, the cell's main contribution is training: users and operators are to be taught that outputs can be false, biased or hallucinated and not to trust them uncritically, and UK071 alone tests whether users interpret outputs correctly. Tools for checking outputs are named (Inspect, automated test harnesses, SHAP and LIME, RAG benchmarks, static analysis of AI-written code) but neither provided nor required, and UK071 explicitly leaves the choice to departments. Only one passage says which outputs reach a human (uncertain cases where automated systems cannot make confident decisions), and none sets a threshold, a reference dataset, a repeatability test or a rule on model versions and prompts.
